device: Night music, then a fast scherzo with no warning
content: The slow movement starts with a calm chorale of muted strings, built from open fourths and fifths. Its middle part is a fast scherzo: "The wild, demonic scherzo, which makes up the middle portion of the movement, begins without warning"
parameters: Form: slow, fast, slow. The full concerto is an arch: fast, slow, fast, slow, fast
example: Bartók, Piano Concerto no. 2 (1931), second movement (Adagio, Presto, Adagio)

device: The piano as a percussion instrument
content: "the solo piano is treated as a percussion instrument". The percussion is near the soloist: "The percussion (including timpani) must be placed directly next to the piano (behind the piano)"
parameters: A pianist: the second concerto is one of the most difficult works of the repertoire
example: Bartók, Piano Concertos no. 1 (1926) and no. 2 (1931)

device: The soloist starts with a cadenza
content: After some bars of the brass, the piano comes in with "an extended cadenza accompanied by percussion and harp". The cadenza gives the first theme: "a savage three-note motto"
In the development, the savage motto becomes a lyrical theme, and the lyrical theme becomes the savage motto: "each one becomes the other"

device: A loud peak, then a sudden pianissimo
content: The energy has its peak in a run of the piano. The run stops on the first note of the orchestra. Then a sudden pianissimo of the full orchestra changes the tempo and the mood
"The rhythms throughout the work are highly irregular and meters change often"
The main theme of the last movement is a fugato that "utilizes orchestral and piano tone-clusters as an integral part of its structure"

The cadenza is not an addition. It carries the recapitulation and goes to the climax of the movement. The orchestra comes back at the peak: "the orchestra announces its return, strings and timpani swelling furiously from p to ff"
parameters: The cadenza is about 5 minutes of a movement of 10 to 12 minutes
example: Prokofiev, Piano Concerto no. 2 (1913, new version 1923), first movement

content: "Bring out the soloist as much as possible by contrast": in tone colour, in register, or in rhythm. The piano can use a register that the orchestra does not use. Rests, plucked basses, and short notes make the orchestra light

"Sometimes use dialogue, sometimes have each accompany the other". In loud passages, the soloist and the orchestra alternate: "This gives the illusion of a confrontation between equals". An orchestra that only murmurs in the background makes the result feeble
example: Belkin's notes; Beethoven, Piano Concerto no. 5, first movement, bar 304 and after
